opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. It's a great question, because I think what draws people to Goodfire is less a single research agenda and more a shared sense that something genuinely strange and important is happening, and that we don't understand it nearly as well as we should.

At the core, there's a scientific curiosity: we've built these systems that can do remarkable things, and we mostly don't know *how* they do them. We train them, we evaluate them from the outside, but the internal computation is largely a black box. A lot of the people here find that almost offensive, in a productive way. It's like having a new kind of mind on the table and just not opening it up. So a big part of the conversation is: what are these models actually representing? What concepts do they learn? How are those concepts organized, and how do they get composed into behavior?

Then there's a second thread that's more engineering-minded, which is where I spend a lot of my time. It's not enough to find interesting structure in a model and write a paper about it. The question is whether that understanding lets you *do* something: debug a model, steer it, edit it, catch failure modes before they show up in deployment. We talk a lot about interpretability as a tool rather than just a lens. If you really understand a system, you should be able to intervene on it in precise ways, and that becomes a pretty demanding test of whether your understanding is real.

And the third thread, which ties it all together, is about where this goes long term. As models get more capable and get deployed in higher-stakes settings, I think it becomes increasingly untenable to rely purely on behavioral testing. You want some way of grounding trust in what's actually happening inside. So there's a safety motivation, but it's not separate from the science or the product. The bet is that those things converge: the better our fundamental understanding, the better our tools, and the better our tools, the more safely and usefully people can build with these systems.

So if you sat in on conversations here, you'd hear people jumping between pretty abstract questions, like what the right unit of analysis even is inside a neural network, and very concrete ones, like how do we make this technique work reliably on a model a customer actually cares about. I think that tension is healthy, and honestly it's a lot of what makes the place fun.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that most of what animates conversations at Goodfire comes from a shared sense that we've built these systems that are genuinely remarkable and we don't actually understand how they work. That gap is kind of uncomfortable if you sit with it, and the people who end up at Goodfire tend to be people who can't stop sitting with it.

So the interests cluster around a few things. One is interpretability as a science, in the sense of really wanting to know what the internal representations are, how features compose, what the circuits look like. There's a curiosity-driven piece that's almost like biology, where you're looking at an organism nobody designed in detail and trying to figure out its anatomy.

But the second piece, which is more distinctive to us, is that we care a lot about whether that understanding can be made useful. Can you take what you learn about the internals of a model and actually do something with it? Steer behavior, debug a failure mode, make a model more reliable in a specific domain, catch something before it ships. A lot of the energy in the room is about closing the loop between understanding and control, rather than treating interpretability as purely an academic exercise.

And then the third thread is a kind of engineering pragmatism. There's a lot of discussion about what methods actually scale, what holds up on frontier-sized models versus toy settings, what you can turn into a tool that a developer or a scientist outside the interpretability community would actually pick up. People argue about that a lot, and I think that tension between rigor and usefulness is what keeps the conversations interesting.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the conversations at Goodfire come from this shared curiosity about what’s actually happening inside neural networks. We can train these systems to do remarkable things, but that doesn’t mean we understand how they’re doing them. What representations are they learning? How do those representations combine to produce behavior? And can we turn that understanding into an ability to shape the systems more deliberately?

That brings together a few different intellectual interests. There’s a scientific impulse to understand intelligence, and an engineering impulse to make something useful out of that understanding. For me, the exciting part is the connection between those two: if we think we’ve understood something inside a model, can we intervene on it and get the change we expect? That’s a way to test our understanding, and potentially a way to build better models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of us are driven by this question of: what is actually going on inside these models? We can train systems that do remarkable things, but our ability to understand how they do those things is still pretty limited. And that’s a fascinating scientific problem, but it’s also a practical one. If we understood the internal mechanisms better, could we make models more reliable? Could we steer them more precisely?

So the conversations tend to sit at that intersection of curiosity and engineering. You want to understand intelligence as a phenomenon, and you want that understanding to give you better tools for working with it.
